idiom_name: JVM class loader + ServiceLoader (Scala 2 runtimeMirror for construction)
implementation_notes: Scala inherits the JVM's mechanism: the configuration names a fully qualified class, the configurator loads it with Class.forName/classLoader.loadClass, and components are published as traits - compiled to interfaces - in an artifact shared with the host; ServiceLoader discovery works exactly as in Java (META-INF/services or module provides). Scala 2 can construct components through scala-reflect: runtimeMirror(getClass.getClassLoader) exposes the classes of that loader and reflectClass(...).reflectConstructor(...).apply(...) instantiates them, including constructors with named or default parameters; Scala 3 projects fall back on java.lang.reflect or compile-time scala.quoted. There is no Scala-level dynamic linking on Scala.js or Scala Native, and no Scala-level unload on the JVM - classes disappear only when their loader becomes unreachable.
pitfalls: scala-reflect is tied to the Scala 2 compiler line and adds a large runtime dependency, and Scala 3 dropped it; prefer a factory function exported by the component or plain java.lang.reflect so the migration does not rewrite the loading path.
The contract trait must come from a parent class loader - a duplicated contract artifact gives two incompatible trait identities and every cast to Component fails.

Scala.js and Scala Native cannot load code at runtime at all, so a cross-built module's 'component configuration' can only be compile-time linking; keep the configurator in the JVM module and the contract platform-neutral.
